findings.title: Dark-theme notification badges put $secondary text on a near-$secondary background
findings.body: .badge-notification sets color to $secondary (line 235, and again on &[href]) and this change sets the dark-theme background to scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%). $secondary is the page background, so that fill is only 30% of the way from the dark background toward white, while the label stays the same dark color. Even if $secondary is pure black the contrast is about 2.5:1; with a typical dark secondary such as #222 it is worse, so base notification counts are illegible in every dark theme. The old scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%) stayed light in dark themes because $primary is already light there, which is why dark $secondary text was readable. new-posts/unread-posts override the background, but any badge that uses the base background does not. Keep a light pill in both themes, or switch the dark-theme text to $primary when the background is derived from $secondary.

findings.title: Embedded-post author link lightness is swapped
findings.body: .embedded-posts .topic-meta-data h5 a was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%). Every other conversion in this PR keeps that lightness on $primary for light themes and uses the complement on $secondary for dark themes, which here would be 30% / 70%. This line instead emits dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)). Light themes therefore render those author links much paler than before and paler than the same treatment in common/base/topic-post.scss, which correctly stayed at 30%. Dark themes get a color only 30% lighter than the dark background, so the names have poor contrast. The .arrow rule on the next line was converted correctly from 60% to 60%/40%, so this swap is not the mapping used elsewhere.

findings.title: Mobile custom-message-length hint inverts the 70% lightness
findings.body: .custom-message-length was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%) and is now dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%)). The light-theme branch must stay at 70%; the dark branch should be scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%). Desktop modal.scss converted the same hint correctly to 70%/30%. On mobile light themes the character-count hint becomes much darker than before and than desktop; on dark themes it becomes a light gray (70% toward white from $secondary) instead of the muted 30% color, so the hint no longer matches across viewports.

findings.title: Mobile topic-map h3 lightness changed from 20% to 50%
findings.body: .topic-map h3 was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%) and is now dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%)). That changes the light-theme color and uses the wrong dark complement; the established mapping is 20% on $primary and 80% on $secondary. Desktop topic-post.scss converted the same h3 correctly to 20%/80%. Mobile topic-map headings become more washed out in light themes, and in dark themes they are a mid-gray instead of the stronger color. The h4 in this same block was already 50% and correctly stayed 50%/50%, so the h3/h4 emphasis difference is lost on mobile and mobile no longer matches desktop.

findings.title: Group member name color changed from 30% to 50% lightness
findings.body: .user-stream .group-member-info .name was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) and is now dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%)). Light themes therefore render member names lighter than before. The dark complement of 30% is scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%), which is what common/base/user.scss uses for .user-small .name. The .title rule immediately below was already 50% and was correctly wrapped as 50%/50%, so names and titles that were intentionally different now share one color in both themes.

findings.title: Mobile group member name color changed from 30% to 50% lightness
findings.body: .user-stream .group-member-info .name was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) and is now dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%)). That regresses the light-theme color and picks the wrong dark-theme value; a 30% source should stay 30% on $primary and use scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%), matching common/base/user.scss .user-small .name. The .title rule just below was already 50% and correctly stayed 50%/50%, so mobile group-member names and titles that used to differ now look the same.

findings.title: Disabled composer textarea text and background collide in dark themes
findings.body: .wmd-input:disabled now uses scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 25%) in dark themes, a dark gray only a quarter of the way from the dark background toward white. The textarea color on line 175 is darken($primary, 40%). In a dark theme $primary is the light text color, so darkening it by 40 points yields a mid-dark gray. For a typical scheme ($primary around #ddd, $secondary around #222) those two land near lightness 47% and 35%, about 1.6:1, so disabled composer text is unreadable. The previous scale-color($primary, $lightness: 75%) stayed near-white in dark themes because $primary is already light, and the same darkened text remained readable on that light field. This $secondary substitution is for muted foregrounds, not for a field whose text is a darkened $primary.

findings.title: Category badge-notification color still scales $primary in dark themes
findings.body: .topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification still sets color to scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%) while the other 50% text colors in this same file (header cells, excerpts, education text) were wrapped as dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%)). In a dark theme this still lightens the already-light $primary, so category notification counts stay brighter than the surrounding muted text instead of getting the dark-theme treatment this change applies everywhere else in the file.
